newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FORECAST-Irish inflation seen remaining benign.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Irish inflation seen remaining benign.

text.p: Irish consumer prices are expected to rise slightly in the quarter to mid-August but the overall inflation picture should remain benign, analysts say.

Forecasts for the mid-August consumer price index, due for release at 1100 GMT (1200 local time) on Thursday, range from a year-on-year growth rate of 1.5 percent to 1.8 percent compared with 1.4 percent in May and 2.4 percent in August last year.
The usual seasonal increase in the cost of foreign holidays is likely to be the main factor in the rise from mid-May levels, analysts said.

Alan McQuaid, economist at Bloxham Stockbrokers, expects services and related expenditure, the component of the CPI index which includes foreign travel, to rise by 0.4 percent in the mid-August quarter.
But overall he expects inflation to remain subdued, rising 0.7 percent on the quarter and 1.6 percent year-on-year.
Food remains an uncertain component with many analysts expecting a rise in food prices after a surprise fall in the third quarter last year.
"The usual thing that can drive it bananas one way or the other is food," said NCB economist Dermot O'Brien.
O'Brien is forecasting a 0.6 percent rise in prices on the quarter for a 1.6 percent increase year-on-year.

"What we've allowed for is an increase in food prices as compared with last year when there was a surprise drop and that's one of the main reasons why the annual rate is ticking up from 1.4 at mid-May to 1.6 percent," he told Reuters.

Depressing the index should be declines in fuel and clothing prices while a fall in mortgage interest rates early in the summer should also help, said Oliver Mangan, economist at Davy Stockbrokers. He expects the overall index to rise by 0.6 percent on the quarter and 1.6 percent year-on-year.
Analysts say a subdued figure should support the long end of the Irish bond market, helping spreads over Germany to narrow.

Some say it should also reassure the interbank market which has been unsettled by strong credit growth fugures in recent months. Data released last week showed that underlying private sector credit grew by 13.7 percent in the year to end-July, well above the central bank's single-digit target.
But analysts say that strength in lending has not fed through to consumer prices to date.
"There's absolutely no sign that this growth in credit, apart from house prices themselves, is spilling over into general inflation," said NCB's O'Brien.
"From that point of view, maybe it should inject a bit of sense into this debate," he added.
But investors in both the bond and interbank markets will be keeping a very close eye on the central bank's quarterly bulletin, also due for release on Thursday.
The bulletin and the ensuing news conference will be closely scanned for any clues to the bank's current views on inflation and the threat posed by strong credit growth.
